text: VOCABULARY OF RHYMES The purpose of this vocabulary of rhymes is to list only such words and pronunciations as are in current good use and as are in keeping with the practice of good poets who have exercised freedom in observing the rules of rhyming.
text_raw:
VOCABULARY OF RHYMES
The purpose of this vocabulary of rhymes is to list only
such words and pronunciations as are in current good use
and as are in keeping with the practice of good poets who
have exercised freedom in observing the rules of rhyming.

text: Obsolete, dialectal, and illiterate words and pronuncia- tions are not recognized.
text_raw:
Obsolete, dialectal, and illiterate words and pronuncia-
tions are not recognized.

text: A few foreign words of frequent occurrence in English speech and writing have been en- tered.
text_raw:
A few foreign words of frequent
occurrence in English speech and writing have been en-
tered.

text: As a rule rhymes "to the eye," as bough and though, are very sparingly given.
text_raw:
As a rule rhymes "to the eye," as bough and
though, are very sparingly given.

text: There are two common forms of rhymes: rhymes of monosyllables or of final accented syllables (called single, or masculine, rhymes); rhymes of two syllables the first of which is accented (called double, or feminine, rhymes), such as pastor, faster, aiding, fading.
text_raw:
There are two common forms of rhymes: rhymes of
monosyllables or of final accented syllables (called single,
or masculine, rhymes); rhymes of two syllables the first of
which is accented (called double, or feminine, rhymes),
such as pastor, faster, aiding, fading.

text: Single, or masculine, rhymes are the more common, and are the only ones listed freely in this vocabulary.
text_raw:
Single, or masculine,
rhymes are the more common, and are the only ones listed
freely in this vocabulary.

text: MASCULINE RHYMES Theory and practice in rhyming.
text_raw:
MASCULINE RHYMES
Theory and practice in rhyming.

text: Theoretically, a rhyme is the correspondence, in two or more words or verses, of terminal sounds beginning with an accented vowel, which, in modern English usage, must be preceded by different consonant sounds, or by a consonant sound or sounds in one case and none in the other.
text_raw:
Theoretically, a rhyme
is the correspondence, in two or more words or verses, of
terminal sounds beginning with an accented vowel, which,
in modern English usage, must be preceded by different
consonant sounds, or by a consonant sound or sounds in
one case and none in the other.

text: In strict rhyme there is, therefore, exact correspondence in sound and also exact correspondence in accent.
text_raw:
In strict rhyme there is,
therefore, exact correspondence in sound and also exact
correspondence in accent.

text: In practice, however, these theoretical standards are not always strictly observed and more or less freedom is exercised even by careful poets.
text_raw:
In practice, however, these
theoretical standards are not always strictly observed and
more or less freedom is exercised even by careful poets.

text: This vocabulary includes many rhymes sanctioned by good usage under the extensions of the rules noted in the following paragraphs.
text_raw:
This vocabulary includes many rhymes sanctioned by
good usage under the extensions of the rules noted in the
following paragraphs.

text: Strictly speaking, single rhymes consist only of monosyllables or of final syllables having a primary accent.
text_raw:
Strictly speaking, single
rhymes consist only of monosyllables or of final syllables
having a primary accent.

text: There are, however, many polysyllables which, having a primary accent on the ante- penult, receive on the final syllable a secondary accent of sufficient strength to make it proper to use these words in single rhymes; thus, accumulate may be used to rhyme with date or create, expedite to rhyme with sight or benight.
text_raw:
There are, however, many
polysyllables which, having a primary accent on the ante-
penult, receive on the final syllable a secondary accent of
sufficient strength to make it proper to use these words in
single rhymes; thus, accumulate may be used to rhyme
with date or create, expedite to rhyme with sight or benight.

text: In polysyllables, such common terminations as -an, -ant, etc., are usually slighted in pronunciation, so that the vowel quality is obscured, as in pelican.
text_raw:
In polysyllables, such common terminations as -an, -ant,
etc., are usually slighted in pronunciation, so that the
vowel quality is obscured, as in pelican.

text: Consequently under -AN, -ANT, etc., this vocabulary restricts its choice of words of more than one syllable to those which have a primary accent on the last syllable or, in the case of poly- syllables accented on the antepenult, an unslurred final syllable, as in sedan, caravan, supplant, epitaph.
text_raw:
Consequently
under -AN, -ANT, etc., this vocabulary restricts its choice of
words of more than one syllable to those which have a
primary accent on the last syllable or, in the case of poly-
syllables accented on the antepenult, an unslurred final
syllable, as in sedan, caravan, supplant, epitaph.

text: Further- more, only monosyllables which, because of their impor- tance to the thought, are likely to carry the speech accent are entered.
text_raw:
Further-
more, only monosyllables which, because of their impor-
tance to the thought, are likely to carry the speech accent
are entered.

text: Certain monosyllabic words usually slurred over in speech, as prepositions and articles, are therefore excluded as not proper to serious verse.
text_raw:
Certain monosyllabic words usually slurred
over in speech, as prepositions and articles, are therefore
excluded as not proper to serious verse.

text: The chief prin- ciple to be observed in exercising freedom regarding cor- respondence of accent is that no rhyme be forced and that accepted pronunciations and customary speech accents be respected.
text_raw:
The chief prin-
ciple to be observed in exercising freedom regarding cor-
respondence of accent is that no rhyme be forced and that
accepted pronunciations and customary speech accents be
respected.

text: In this connection, it should be noted that in many words of the same spelling and derivation, as con- tract, the accent is not placed on the same syllable in each part of speech, and that in others, as the noun recess, a change in sense may mean a change in accent.
text_raw:
In this connection, it should be noted that in
many words of the same spelling and derivation, as con-
tract, the accent is not placed on the same syllable in each
part of speech, and that in others, as the noun recess, a
change in sense may mean a change in accent.

text: For this reason, use of the main vocabulary of the dictionary will sometimes be necessary in determining the part of speech or the sense in which a word may be used as a rhyme.
text_raw:
For this
reason, use of the main vocabulary of the dictionary will
sometimes be necessary in determining the part of speech
or the sense in which a word may be used as a rhyme.

text: Strictly speaking, the termi- nal vowel sounds should exactly correspond, but poets i sometimes use rhymes in which the vowels are not exact homophones.
text_raw:
Strictly speaking, the termi-
nal vowel sounds should exactly correspond, but poets i
sometimes use rhymes in which the vowels are not exact
homophones.

text: In the vocabulary of rhymes, broad dif- ferences in terminal sounds, as in words ending in -age, are shown by multiple entries and multiple lists of words, but slight differences in the quality of terminal vowels are not so differentiated.
text_raw:
In the vocabulary of rhymes, broad dif-
ferences in terminal sounds, as in words ending in -age, are
shown by multiple entries and multiple lists of words, but

text: Words differing but slightly are usu- ally, as at -ANT, included under one entry.
text_raw:
Words differing but slightly are usu-

text: Those who seek close or delicate correspondence in sounds should con- sult the main vocabulary and the numbered sections of the Guide to Pronunciation to which cross reference is made.

Those who
seek close or delicate correspondence in sounds should con-

text: Rhymes by contraction, elision, etc. The final two syl- lables of a word are often pronounced like a single syllable with a long vowel sound, by slurring over or slighting one of the syllables in the pronunciation, or by dropping a consonant or vowel.
text_raw:
Rhymes by contraction, elision, etc. The final two syl-
lables of a word are often pronounced like a single syllable
with a long vowel sound, by slurring over or slighting one
of the syllables in the pronunciation, or by dropping a
consonant or vowel.

text: Thus plyer, higher, as ordinarily pro- nounced, may be used to rhyme with lyre, fire; the poetical o'er to rhyme with lore, roar; the poetical ne'er to rhyme with care, stair.
text_raw:
Thus plyer, higher, as ordinarily pro-
nounced, may be used to rhyme with lyre, fire; the poetical

text: For some words, more than one pronunciation is recognized as being in good usage, and the more common of these, when they can be used in single rhymes in either or both pronunciations, are given in this vocabulary in each group with which they may rhyme; thus, trait (see pron. in main vocab.) is given under -ATE and -AY, wrath under -ATH and -OTH, etc. This rule does not hold for foreign words that have two pro- nunciations.

text: Only that part of the word or last syllable is considered which corresponds in sound with that of its rhymes, and this part of each word is treated as a termination or ending.

text: All of these termina- tions must, therefore, begin with the last sounded vowel or diphthong of the word; hence any particular word with its rhymes can be readily found in this vocabulary by looking for such ending.

FEMININE RHYMES
Theoretically, feminine rhymes occur at the ends of
lines in trochaic, amphibrachic, and dactylic meter; actu-
ally, they often also occur when the poet, for one reason
or another, wishes to add a hypermetrical syllable or syl-
lables.

text: They are also called double (or triple) rhymes because there must be correspondence in sound and accent between the last accented syllable and the following syl- lable or syllables.

They are also called double (or triple) rhymes
because there must be correspondence in sound and accent
between the last accented syllable and the following syl-
lable or syllables.

text: The rule for masculine rhymes requir- ing a consonantal difference (sometimes by omission of one consonant) before the rhyming sounds holds good here for the accented syllables of the feminine rhyme but not for the unaccented syllables, which must be identical in sound; thus tabard rhymes with scabbard, feather with heather, pastor with master, furious with penurious.

ORTHOGRAPHY
Spelling changes advocated by Noah Webster in his |
Dictionary (1828) have had considerable influence upon
orthography, especially in the United States.

text: These changes were proposed by him chiefly on the basis of etymology and of analogy with the dual object, first, of making the words correspond, as far as practicable, with their primitive forms in order to reveal more ob- viously their etymological affinities, and second, of re- ducing the number of anomalies and exceptional cases.
text_raw:
These
changes were proposed by him chiefly on the basis of
etymology and of analogy with the dual object, first,
of making the words correspond, as far as practicable,
with their primitive forms in order to reveal more ob-
viously their etymological affinities, and second, of re-
ducing the number of anomalies and exceptional cases.

text: It is to be observed that many of these deviations from the usage of his time were not innovations, but restorations of older forms which were once gener- ally employed.

It is to be observed that many of these deviations

forth on this continent a new nation, conceived in liberty,
and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created
equal.
